extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, students and critics of dramatic poetry (writers of tragedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidelines for composing classical tragedy: structuring plot and incidents, creating character, and using recognition/reversal to produce pity and fear. Aimed at dramatists and readers evaluating tragic poems/plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic plots (probable/necessary sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: I call a plot 'episodic' in which the episodes or acts succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad poets compose such pieces by their own fault, often stretching plots for show (competition) and thereby breaking natural continuity. Plots should exhibit probable/necessary sequence so events follow one another logically rather than as disconnected episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy imitates a complete action producing pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of a complete action, of events terrible and pitiful; the effect is best when events come by surprise and (at the same time) follow from one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tragic 'wonder' is heightened when events seem designed rather than accidental; coincidences are most striking when they have an air of design (example: statue of Myron at Argos). Construct plots so the emotional effects (pity/fear) arise from the action's internal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer complex plots (involving reversal/recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are either Simple or Complex. A Simple action is continuous with change of fortune without Reversal or Recognition. A Complex action includes Reversal (peripeteia) or Recognition (anagnorisis) or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots (with reversal/recognition) are superior because they produce stronger tragic effects; aim to have such elements arise from the plot's internal structure rather than contrivances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal (Peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal is a change by which a train of action produces the opposite of the intended effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversal must still conform to probability or necessity. Examples: in Oedipus the messenger intends to comfort but reveals the truth and causes the opposite effect; in Lynceus Danaus goes to slay him but is killed and Lynceus saved. Use reversal to turn expectations in a way that is still plausible within the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge producing love or hate between persons destined for good or bad fortune; recognition combined with Reversal produces pity or fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best form of recognition is coincident with reversal (e.g., Oedipus). Recognition of persons is most intimately connected to plot; it can also be of deeds or signified objects. Aim for recognition moments that are integral to the causal chain of the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic Incident (on-stage destructive/painful actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tragic Incident is a destructive or painful action — death on the stage, bodily agony, wounds and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic incidents are one of the parts that turn upon surprise; they should be used where appropriate to heighten pity/fear but handled artistically (not merely spectacularly) and integrated into the plot's causal order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of quantitative/structural parts (prologue, episode, exodos, choric song)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into parts: Prologue (precedes Parodos), Episode (between complete choric songs), Exodos (no choric song after it), and the Choric parts (Parodos, Stasimon); Commos is a joint lamentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These structural parts are common to plays; understand their definitions and how they function in ordering incidents and the chorus' role. Use them to organize the unfolding action and choric commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper choice of protagonist (middle character, hamartia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune should not be the spectacle of a virtuous man brought from prosperity to adversity (nor of a bad man to prosperity, nor the downfall of an utter villain). The protagonist should be between extremes — not eminently good and just, nor utterly wicked — whose misfortune is brought about not by vice but by some error or frailty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pity is aroused by unmerited misfortune, fear by misfortune like our own; thus the protagonist should be renowned/prosperous yet flawed by error (hamartia). Examples: Oedipus, Thyestes. This produces effective tragic emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and singleness of issue (single plot focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed plot should be single in its issue, rather than double; the change of fortune should be from good to bad and come about as the result not of vice but of error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sprawling double-threads; tragedies are strongest when focused on a single causal chain (often the fortunes of a single house/family). The practice of the stage demonstrates greater tragic effect when focus is narrow and unified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner structural causes preferred over spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacular means, but they may also result from the inner structure of the piece — which is the better way and indicates a superior poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot ought to be so constructed that even without visual spectacle the tale will thrill and melt. Reliance on spectacle to produce the monstrous is less artistic and not proper to tragedy; favor mimetic structural methods that evoke pity/fear via plot and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances that arouse pity and fear (relations of persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of tragic effect must happen between persons who are friends, enemies, or indifferent; strongest effect arises when the tragic incident occurs between those who are near or dear to one another (brother killing brother, son his father, mother her son, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The emotional impact is greatest in familial or closely bound relationships; poets should seek such situations (while not necessarily violating traditional legendary frameworks) and handle them with invention and skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of horror deeds: three modes and ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: The deed of horror may be (1) done consciously with knowledge of the persons, (2) done in ignorance with the tie discovered afterwards (best), or (3) about to be done but discovered before acting (worst).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best tragic arrangement is when the deed is perpetrated in ignorance and discovered later — produces startling discovery without gratuitous shock. The worst (about to act and then not acting) is shocking but not tragic because no disaster follows. Examples: Medea (conscious), Oedipus (done in ignorance discovered later), Haemon/Antigone (threat but not enacted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character aims: goodness, propriety, verisimilitude, consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: In respect of Character there are four things to be aimed at: (1) it must be good (purpose/ moral intent), (2) propriety (appropriate to sex/status/role), (3) true to life (verisimilitude distinct from goodness), (4) consistency (a character may be inconsistent in type but must be consistently inconsistent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodness is relative to each class (women/slaves can be 'good'); propriety demands fitting traits (e.g., manly valor inappropriate as a general female trait); verisimilitude requires believable behavior; consistency requires internal coherence even for a capricious character. Avoid gratuitously bad, indecorous, or inconsistent portrayals (examples noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity/probability governs actions and character
rubrics_metrics.description: As in the structure of the plot, so too in the portrayal of character, the poet should always aim either at the necessary or the probable: a person of a given character should speak or act by rule of necessity or probability; the unravelling must arise out of the plot itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on irrational elements inside the action; if irrationality exists (e.g., Oedipus' case) it should lie outside the proper scope of the tragedy. Ensure cause/effect and character motivation obey plausibility to produce convincing catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid internal deus ex machina
rubrics_metrics.description: The unravelling of the plot must not be brought about by the deus ex machina — which should be employed only for events external to the drama (antecedent or subsequent events beyond human knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist contrived external rescues or explanations that resolve the plot internally; such devices weaken the tragic imitation. Use deus ex machina only for matters outside the dramatic world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ennoble types while preserving likeness (poetic elevation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since Tragedy imitates persons who are above the common level, the poet should follow good portrait-painters: reproduce the distinctive form of the original while making a likeness true to life yet more beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve characteristic traits of characters (irascibility, indolence, etc.) but 'ennoble' them — make types clearer and more elevated (example: Achilles as portrayed by Homer and Agathon). This contributes to the tragic dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition forms ranked by artistry
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions occur by signs/tokens (least artistic), by a turn of incident (better), by poet-invented revelations (artificial), by memory/feeling awakened by an object, or by process of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Least artistic: explicit tokens used solely for proof (e.g., necklaces, scars used as formal proof). Better: recognition through incident/scene (e.g., bath scene in Odyssey). Worse/artificial: characters simply declare identities because the poet needs it (voice of the shuttle example). Preferred: memory/affect or logical reasoning recognitions (examples: Odysseus' scar, the nurse/herdsmen, reasoning in Choephori). Choose methods that arise naturally and enhance art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tokens/signs as recognition (use sparingly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some recognitions depend on signs: congenital marks (spears/marks), acquired tokens (scars, necklaces, little ark).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tokens admit degrees of skill — Odysseus' scar is handled well by nurse/herdsmen differently. Formal proofs or tokens introduced expressly for discovery are less artistic; prefer recognitions that arise from incident or memory for higher artistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of chorus and sensory appeals (concomitants but not essentials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to the senses (spectacle, chorus, music) are concomitants of poetry and offer room for error but are not among the essentials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While sensory elements can support the effect, poets should not neglect them; yet the primary source of tragic pleasure must be imitation that produces pity and fear — sensory aids should complement, not substitute, plot and character construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude irrational elements from internal action
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the action there must be nothing irrational; if irrationality cannot be excluded it should be outside the scope of the tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrational elements (that violate probability/necessity) undermine the imitation and should be avoided unless they belong to events outside the dramatic world (example: certain aspects of Oedipus are treated as external).
